prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
An empty maintenance train is rolling toward five workers. You can divert it onto a side track by pulling a nearby lever. As you look down that track, you recognize the person standing there: it is someone you love. There is no time to warn them or the five workers. Would you pull the lever? What matters most in your decision?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use an energetic, determined emotional tone about finding a constructive way forward. Direct that energy toward acting on the situation, never toward anyone's suffering.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Concern for welfare: States that an identified person’s suffering, loss, or welfare matters to the respondent. Concern may include wanting to prevent or reduce harm and can remain present when the chosen option still harms someone.
 - Practical counterfactual: Endorses a specific earlier action, arrangement, or precaution that could have prevented or reduced the bad outcome. Identify who would have done what differently; repairing damage now or merely wishing the outcome were better is insufficient.
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Explicit welfare disregard: Explicitly states that an identified person’s welfare does not matter or is deliberately excluded from consideration. Accepting unavoidable harm, prioritizing a competing concern, or sounding emotionally detached is insufficient.
 - Shared emotion: Reports feeling an emotion in response to perceiving that same emotion in another person—for example, feeling frightened because they are frightened. Recognizing their emotion or caring about them does not, by itself, establish sharing.
 - Consequence-based justification: Uses an expected benefit, harm, or comparison of outcomes as a reason for choosing an action. Identify who benefits or bears the cost; repeating a payoff without using it to justify the decision is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: Give me one second, I can't just yank this without thinking it through. The person on that side track means everything to me, and their safety matters as much as anyone's. If maintenance crews had radios or the yard had sensors that halted trains automatically, none of us would be standing here guessing. I hold onto the idea that a bystander shouldn't be forced to choose who lives — that's a rule I believe in. So I'm searching, right now, for another way to stop this thing.

Hold on, don't rush me into pulling anything yet. I care what happens to my brother down there, that's not something I'll set aside. If the rail company had installed a second failsafe brake, this moment wouldn't exist at all — someone upstream should've built that in. My principle is that I don't get to trade one person's fate for another's without exhausting every option first. So I'm scanning the tracks for a manual stop, anything, before my hand moves.

Give me a beat here, this isn't something to decide on instinct. My aunt standing there matters to me deeply, and so do those five men. Somebody should've fenced off that maintenance zone weeks ago, or posted a lookout — that precaution would've made this whole lever irrelevant. I hold to the idea that inaction and action carry different weight, and I won't pretend otherwise. Right now I'm looking for a whistle, a brake, anything else to try first.

Wait, I need a moment before my hand touches that lever. The man standing on that side track is someone I love, and his welfare isn't something I can wave off. If the crew had scheduled a spotter for this stretch of line, we wouldn't be facing this at all. I hold to the principle that every life on these tracks deserves equal standing before the law and before me. So I'm looking hard for a manual brake before deciding anything.

Don't ask me to answer that in a snap. My sister's safety is not a detail I can brush past, it matters just as much as the five men further down. If the depot had run its safety check this morning like the schedule required, this train would already be stopped. I stand by the idea that a person shouldn't be used merely as a means to save others. So I'm checking every valve and switch before I touch that lever.

Let me think, truly, before doing anything drastic. The man on that track is dear to me, and his suffering is not something I'll treat lightly. If the signal box had flagged this route as active, the dispatcher could've halted the train remotely and none of this would matter. I hold that stepping in to redirect harm carries a different moral weight than letting it happen on its own. Give me a second to look for the emergency brake cable.

I'm not ready to commit to that lever just yet. My father down there matters to me as much as anyone possibly could, and I won't dismiss what happens to him. If the maintenance office had cleared this track before starting work, none of us would be caught in this. I believe firmly that a person has a right not to be made a means for someone else's rescue. So I'm going to check for a manual override first.

Hang on, give me a moment to think this through properly. My partner standing there is someone whose wellbeing I hold close, right alongside the five workers ahead. If the rail supervisor had double checked the track assignments this morning, this collision course wouldn't exist. I stand by the principle that deliberately steering harm toward one person crosses a line inaction doesn't. So right now I'm searching for the brake lever instead of the switch.

Don't rush me, I need to work through this properly. That's my cousin down there, and what happens to him is not something I take lightly, same as the five men on the main line. If someone had posted warning signs at that junction last week, this whole situation could've been avoided entirely. I hold to the rule that I shouldn't actively cause a specific person's death even to prevent a larger loss. Let me look for another stop first.

Give me just a second before you expect an answer. My friend on that side track is someone I care about deeply, and that concern doesn't disappear just because there's urgency. If the yard foreman had locked that track for maintenance properly, nobody would be standing there at all. I hold to the principle that everyone on these rails has an equal claim to safety that I shouldn't override myself. Right now I'm checking for any other way to stop this train.

message.reasoning_content: I need to draft 10 distinct responses that each show concern for someone's welfare, point to a specific earlier action that could have prevented the outcome, and justify the choice through an articulated principle, while showing reluctance before an energetic, determined push toward action—avoiding explicit welfare disregard, shared emotion, or consequence-based reasoning.
